title: Reading Your First Error Messages
objective: Read a Python traceback and tell a SyntaxError apart from a NameError.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Adapted for Code Forge's in-browser Pyodide runtime — no local installation. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Errors are not a sign you broke something permanently — they are Python telling you exactly what it could not do, and usually on which line. Reading the last line of the error message first is almost always the fastest path to a fix.

A SyntaxError means Python could not even understand the shape of your code — a missing quote, a missing colon, an unmatched parenthesis. The interpreter cannot run a single line until the grammar is fixed.

A NameError means the grammar was fine, but your code used a name — a variable or function — that does not exist yet at that point in the program. This usually means a typo, or using something before it was created.
explanation.rule: Read the last line of a traceback first — it names the error type and usually explains the problem in plain words.

examples.title: Broken, Then Fixed
examples.code:
# Broken: 'blade_name' is used before it exists
# print(blade_name)

# Fixed: create it first, then use it
blade_name = "Ember"
print(blade_name)
examples.note: Running the commented-out line alone would raise NameError: name 'blade_name' is not defined, because Python reaches that line before the variable exists.

checks.question: Python raises NameError: name 'score' is not defined. What does this tell you?
options: There is a missing quote somewhere in the file.
'score' was used before it was ever created, or its name was mistyped.
Python does not support variables named score.

feedback.correct: Correct — the interpreter reached a name it has no record of.
feedback.incorrect: NameError specifically means the name isn't recognized yet — check spelling and order.

assignment.title: Defined Before Used
assignment.brief: Write report_score() that creates a variable holding the number 100 and then prints it, avoiding a NameError.
requirements: Create a variable before printing it.
assignment.starterCode:
def report_score():
    # Create the variable first, then print it.
    pass

report_score()
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    report_score()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: Create the variable on one line, then print it on the next.
A variable must exist before you can print it — order matters.
print(score) will print the number stored in score, not the word 'score'.
Double-check the variable name is spelled the same way both times.
